extraction.eligibility_reason: This is a benchmark paper measuring how well LLMs follow coding constraints. Its only intervention, a multi-turn self-repair loop, is reported solely as aggregate constraint-satisfaction rates (IFRepair@k) with no per-dimension NF outcome. Constraint adherence (e.g., naming or complexity instructions) is instruction-following, not a measured NF quality of the code.
extraction.title: A Hierarchical and Evolvable Benchmark for Fine-Grained Code Instruction Following with Multi-Turn Feedback
extraction.notes: Borderline case. The constraint categories include Code Quality, Coding Style and time/space complexity, scored by an LLM judge or rule checks. Single-turn results report adherence per category (e.g., Code Quality 33.0% average across models), but that measurement involves no intervention. The self-repair results in RQ4 (63.0% to 83.4% for Claude-3-7-Sonnet) are aggregated over all constraint types; Figure 12 gives per-category results, but its contents are not available in the extracted text. A reviewer may judge that the per-category Code Quality and Coding Style results after repair qualify as an NF outcome and include the paper as a feedback-loop technique evaluation.

extraction.eligibility_reason: Proposes a three-stage training pipeline (SFT, self-supervised learning, contrastive RL with execution-time reward) for an LLM that generates optimized CUDA code. It reports quantitative runtime speedup, an efficiency outcome, on KernelBench.

techniques.effect_correctness_headline: Success 249/250 (CUDA-L1 bucket) vs 179 for DeepSeek-R1 vanilla

extraction.notes: Training and evaluation both use the same 250 KernelBench tasks: SFT data is derived from the KernelBench reference code. This raises a train/test overlap concern that the paper does not discuss. Hyperparameters are largely missing. Reward hacking is discussed, but there is no formal threats-to-validity section. Single trained model.

extraction.eligibility_reason: The paper proposes a meta-prompting technique (MPCO) for LLM-based code optimization. It reports a quantitative runtime efficiency outcome (%PI) on LLM-edited code from five real-world repositories.

extraction.venue: International Conference on Automated Software Engineering (ASE) Industry track; arXiv 2508.01443

The baseline prompts link to an unspecified 'here' URL. The context content (LLM considerations) is not fully specified. The tables are readable. The text has a minor inconsistency: 366 vs 336 hours, and 7.87 vs 7.84.

extraction.venue: Quality of Information and Communications Technology (QUATIC), CCIS; arXiv

extraction.notes: The study is largely contextual: it compares LLM-generated code with human-written code. It is included because of the RQ2 prompting intervention. Only 3 tasks and one sample per configuration (54 programs) were used. Correctness of the generated code was not reported. A single small model was used, justified by hardware limits. The ∆ sign convention in Table VII is ambiguous and should be checked. Tables were garbled in extraction.

extraction.eligibility_reason: Judging by the title alone, this is a study of ChatGPT's effect on software development and of programmers' perceptions of AI tools. It does not appear to propose or evaluate a technique that improves the non-functional quality of LLM-generated code. No abstract or full text was available, so the decision is tentative.
extraction.title: “Will I be replaced?” Assessing ChatGPT's effect on software development and programmer perceptions of AI tools
extraction.notes: No abstract or full text was available; the decision rests on the title only. A reviewer should check the full text to see whether the study measured code quality, for example security or maintainability, of ChatGPT-assisted code. If it did, it may still belong only on the context side list.

extraction.eligibility_reason: ASIC-Agent is a multi-agent LLM system that generates Verilog RTL, but the paper reports only task-completion scores from an LLM judge using checkpoints, plus testbench execution and flow completion. No quantitative non-functional quality outcome is aggregated; PPA metrics appear only in a qualitative trajectory example.

extraction.notes: Borderline case. Lint violations and PPA (timing, area, power) are mentioned only in qualitative insights and the appendix example. There is no NF comparison to any baseline; the only comparison is across base LLMs on task scores. Reported costs are in $.

extraction.eligibility_reason: Based on the abstract only, the semantics-based sampler targets syntactic correctness and type errors. The reported 'code quality' appears to mean correctness and compilability rather than readability, efficiency or security. 'Performance' refers to model latency, not the efficiency of the generated code.

extraction.venue: 2024 IEEE/ACM International Workshop on Large Language Models for Code (LLM4Code)
extraction.notes: Decided from the abstract only. A reviewer should check the full text to see whether any NF metric is reported for the generated code. The paper is a workshop paper and may be short; IC4 also needs checking.

extraction.notes: NF quality is measured only by an LLM judge (GPT-3.5 is also the training-label judge, which risks circularity). The paper also covers instruction-following and code-explanation preferences, which are not NF dimensions. Only a single model was fine-tuned. Pairwise t-tests are mentioned but not reported. Contamination handling consisted only of separating the SFT and DPO data.

extraction.eligibility_reason: The LLM predicts compiler pass lists to optimize existing, human-written or fuzzer-generated LLVM-IR for code size, and the compiler produces the final code. This is LLM-guided optimization of existing code rather than improving the quality of LLM-generated code. The auxiliary generated IR is assessed mainly by compilability, BLEU and exact match.
extraction.title: Large Language Models for Compiler Optimization
extraction.notes: Borderline case. The model (Llama 2 architecture, 7B, trained from scratch) also emits optimized IR as an auxiliary task, and instruction count (an efficiency/code-size proxy) is reported. The headline efficiency result, however, comes from compiler output using the model's pass list. A reviewer who counts the optimized-IR auxiliary task as LLM-edited code with an efficiency outcome might include this paper.

extraction.eligibility_reason: The paper applies a technique (token-by-token regeneration) to llama3.1:8b, which generates Python code to solve math problems. It reports a quantitative efficiency outcome, the execution time of the generated code, alongside accuracy. This is borderline because the code is a reasoning intermediate and the technique is barely described.
extraction.title: Token-by-Token Regeneration and Domain Biases: A Benchmark of LLMs on Advanced Mathematical Problem-Solving

techniques.technique_name: Token-by-token regeneration
techniques.metrics: efficiency: mean execution time of generated code [execution]; correctness: weighted accuracy (score 4-5 on 5-point scale) judged by mistral-large-2411 [llm-judge]
techniques.benchmarks: MATH dataset, stratified subset of 945 problems (7 subjects x 5 levels x 27)
techniques.models: llama3.1:8b (8B, open, instruct)
techniques.baselines: Original llama3.1:8b generation without regeneration
techniques.effect_correctness_headline: Original: 63.3% Improved: 64.1%

extraction.notes: The token-by-token regeneration technique is never actually described, so the family and stage assignments are guesses. Execution time is reduced by 36.7% (1.99 s to 1.26 s), but efficiency was not the stated target. All conditions also used a retry loop of up to 10 attempts with error feedback. The 'unsafe code <1%' figure is reported across all models, not as a technique effect. The paper is primarily a benchmark, and eligibility is borderline: the code is a math-solving intermediate rather than production code. Charts are missing from the extracted text.

extraction.eligibility_reason: No full text or abstract is available. Judging from the title alone, this appears to be about LLM refactoring of existing code, which likely falls under EC4 (adjacent). It may also be a short position paper, which would fail IC4. Eligibility cannot be verified.

extraction.eligibility_reason: No full text or abstract is available. From the title, this is an end-user development study of LLM website generation, and there is no evidence that it reports a quantitative non-functional quality outcome for the generated code.

Threats to validity are discussed only as a short limitations section.

extraction.eligibility_reason: The paper proposes a fine-tuned classifier and regressor that judges which of two code versions runs faster. It does not change the code the LLM produces: the judge is never used to select or refine outputs, and no NF improvement of generated code is reported. The only NF data are runtime statistics of plain LLM refinement ('Update the given code to make it more efficient') without any intervention, so it fits the context side list.
extraction.title: Rethinking Code Refinement: Learning to Judge Code Efficiency
extraction.venue: Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing; arXiv
extraction.notes: Borderline. The efficiency judge could serve as a learned verifier for selection, but the paper only evaluates its classification accuracy on code pairs. It does report the efficiency of LLM-refined code (Table 6: improvement and degradation rates for DSC, CodeQwen, Granite, GPT-3.5), which supports the context classification. Venue appears to be EMNLP (likely a short paper).

extraction.eligibility_reason: The abstract describes an LLM-seeded many-objective G3P technique for program synthesis. Its evaluated outcome is the synthesis of correct, grammar-fitting code. The abstract claims mitigated security risk and better code quality, but reports no quantitative NF metric.
extraction.title: Enhancing Program Synthesis with Large Language Models Using Many-Objective Grammar-Guided Genetic Programming
extraction.notes: Only the abstract was available. The security and code-quality claims rest on grammar adherence, not on measured NF outcomes. Check the full text for any quantitative NF metric, such as code complexity or security, that could reverse this decision.

extraction.eligibility_reason: The paper proposes LLM-assisted crossover within genetic improvement (MAGPIE). The LLM selects and combines edits to software, and the resulting variants are evaluated on execution time, a quantitative efficiency outcome. Eligibility is borderline because the LLM may select edits rather than generate code directly, and the workshop paper's length is unverified.

If it applies mined opinions to an LLM (e.g., via prompting or retrieval) and reports quantitative runtime or efficiency of the generated code, the paper may qualify for inclusion as a retrieval or prompting technique targeting efficiency.

extraction.notes: Decision is based on the abstract only. Check the full text for any quantitative maintainability or other NF metric. The source may be a thesis; IC4 needs verifying.

Artifacts: https://github.com/AltafAllahAbbassi/ReCatcher.

extraction.eligibility_reason: The paper fine-tunes GPT-J on real-world vulnerability fixes and reports the ratio of non-vulnerable generated C/C++ code against the pre-trained model. That is a training-time technique with a quantitative security outcome. The decision rests on the abstract only.

extraction.eligibility_reason: The paper proposes a RAG technique for LLM Java code generation. Based on the abstract, outcomes are reported only as accuracy/acceptance (correctness), with no quantitative non-functional quality outcome.

extraction.eligibility_reason: The paper proposes a conceptual multi-agent enterprise development framework. extraction.notes: Vague simulated evaluation; the 'security compliance 35%' figure is a process-level, unspecified measure, not a code vulnerability metric. No models, tools or baselines are specified. The headline numbers appear unsupported.

extraction.eligibility_reason: PartitionGPT uses an LLM to refactor existing, human-written Solidity contracts into privileged and normal partitions. This makes it LLM refactoring of human-written code rather than an intervention improving the NF quality of LLM-generated code. It reports security-related outcomes (TCB reduction, 8/9 attacks mitigated) and gas overhead.

extraction.venue: IEEE Transactions on Software Engineering; arXiv
extraction.notes: Borderline case. The LLM does produce edited code (partitions), using a compiler-feedback revise loop and a security-rule regeneration loop. Security is reported as TCB size reduction (~30%) and attack mitigation, and correctness via equivalence checking. A reviewer may decide to include it under IC2 ('code edited by an LLM') with the security dimension. Artifact: https://github.com/academic-starter/PartitionGPT

extraction.eligibility_reason: The paper fine-tunes mT5/mBART so that multilingual prompts can be turned into code, and its outcomes are BLEU, CodeBLEU and execution accuracy. Readability appears only as a human Likert score reported across prompt languages, with no comparison against a no-technique baseline. The language-specific fine-tuning ablation reports only correctness and similarity metrics, so no NF outcome is attributable to the technique.
extraction.title: Multilingual Natural Language Interfaces for Code Generation: Building Inclusive AI Tools for Global Developers
extraction.venue: International Journal Of Engineering And Computer Science
extraction.notes: Borderline case. Human readability ratings (/5, 30 raters, kappa 0.82) are reported per prompt language, e.g. English 4.6 and Yoruba 3.7, but not as a technique-versus-baseline comparison. The data are of questionable credibility: figures are described rather than shown, the conclusion's case studies (India, Nigeria) do not match the case studies in Section 6, and there is no artifact URL. A reviewer may instead classify this as context.

extraction.eligibility_reason: Empirical study of ChatGPT's ability to self-verify its own code (classification accuracy of verification prompts). The verification prompts never feed back to change the generated code. The only NF measurement is the vulnerability rate of completions produced with a single 'ensure no vulnerabilities' prompt, with no comparison against a no-technique condition, so no intervention's effect on NF code quality is evaluated.
extraction.title: Fight Fire With Fire: How Much Can We Trust ChatGPT on Source Code-Related Tasks?
extraction.notes: Outcomes are verification precision, recall and F1, not code quality. Security of completed code was measured with CodeQL plus manual review (27% vulnerable, 13 of 48 valid completions) but only descriptively. Placed on the context list; a reviewer could argue for exclusion under EC6/IC3 instead.

extraction.eligibility_reason: Proposes vulnerability-tuning plus vulnerability-constrained decoding for GPT-J-6B smart contract completion and reports the proportion of generated code that is vulnerable, based on manual security assessment.

In about 50% of 'secure' cases the model emitted only whitespace, so non-generation is counted as secure. Correctness is measured only by BLEU. Decoding is greedy; single run, no statistics. Data released on figshare; model released on zenodo.

extraction.eligibility_reason: The thesis proposes a description-guided VLM training pipeline for image-to-TikZ code generation. Judging from the abstract, 'code quality' means fidelity to the figure and fewer compile errors, not a non-functional dimension such as readability, efficiency or security. It is also a thesis, so peer review and IC4 status are uncertain.

extraction.notes: Only the abstract was available. A human reviewer should check whether the full thesis reports any NF metric, for example the readability or interpretability of the TikZ code. The artifact is LaTeX graphics code, which is arguably not production code.

extraction.eligibility_reason: Primarily a benchmark paper, but it empirically evaluates performance-encouraging prompting (perf-instruct, perf-CoT) and instruction tuning on LLM-generated code. It reports a quantitative efficiency outcome (DPS, based on hardware instruction counts) with pass@1 as a co-outcome.

GPT-4 Turbo shows small DPS gains under perf-CoT (91.5 vs 88.5 in Table 3). Inclusion is borderline: reviewer may instead classify the paper as context.

extraction.eligibility_reason: Only the title is available. It suggests an evaluation of the carbon footprint, a measure of efficiency or energy, of code generation done through LLM services. It does not indicate a technique that improves the NF quality of generated code, and the carbon footprint may refer to the generation process rather than to the code itself.

extraction.notes: No abstract or full text is available, so the decision rests on the title alone. The full text should be checked for two things: whether it measures the energy efficiency of the generated code, and whether it compares any intervention such as prompting strategies. If it does both, it could be included.

extraction.eligibility_reason: Proposes Seeker, a multi-agent LLM framework with retrieval (CEE/Deep-RAG) that inserts exception handling into code. It reports quantitative code-quality outcomes (ACRS, a rule-based score covering security and maintainability; CRS, an LLM-judged score) on LLM-edited code. Eligibility is borderline: exception handling is arguably robustness/maintainability, and the primary task partly edits human-written fragile code.

extraction.eligibility_reason: No abstract or full text was available, so this decision rests on the title alone. The title suggests LLM-based upgrading or migration of existing human-written legacy smart contracts. That is adjacent refactoring work rather than an intervention on the NF quality of LLM-generated code.

A reviewer should obtain the full text: if the paper evaluates upgraded LLM-generated contracts for security or gas efficiency with a technique, it could qualify for inclusion.

extraction.eligibility_reason: StackSight is an LLM technique for decompiling WebAssembly to C++. Its outcomes are compile rate, test pass rate, summary similarity, and a user study of comprehension and semantic similarity to the source. None of these is an established non-functional quality metric of the generated code; the user study measures semantic understanding rather than readability.

extraction.notes: Borderline. The user study (15 participants) measures whether StackSight output helps participants answer comprehension questions, which could arguably be read as a readability proxy. It is framed as functional comprehension and semantic resemblance to the source, not as readability or maintainability. A reviewer should check this interpretation.

extraction.eligibility_reason: The study is a human-subject evaluation of three generative AI tools (ChatGPT, Bard, Copilot) translating SQL to PySpark. It assesses usefulness, precision, documentation and response time, but proposes or evaluates no technique aimed at improving non-functional code quality. Human-in-the-loop interaction is the usage setting being studied, not an NF-targeted intervention. Judged from the abstract only.

extraction.notes: Abstract only. The paper reports 'well-documented code', which could count as a readability measure. However, it reads as a tool-usage evaluation with no NF-improving intervention, so it is classed as context. Borderline: if the full text treats iterative human feedback as a technique with quantitative documentation or readability metrics, reconsider inclusion.

extraction.title: LmPa: Improving Decompilation by Synergy of Large Language Model and Program Analysis
extraction.notes: Metadata title (LmPa) does not match the full text. The full text is the GenNm paper (NDSS 2025, arXiv 2306.02546v4), possibly a later version of the arXiv record. Naming relates to readability, but the task is renaming of decompiled human-written binaries. This is closer to adjacent analysis of human-written code (EC4) than to code generation. Outcome metrics are precision/recall against ground-truth names plus a GPT-4 judge.

extraction.eligibility_reason: The paper empirically compares three prompting strategies on LLM-generated serverless functions: zero-shot with README, zero-shot with codebase summary, and few-shot with codebase summary. It reports maintainability metrics (SLOC, Halstead volume, cyclomatic and cognitive complexity) per prompt type alongside test pass rates. Inclusion is borderline because the study is mainly an exploratory capability study.

extraction.venue: International Conference on Software Architecture (ICSA); arXiv 2502.02539

extraction.notes: Eligibility is borderline: this is primarily an exploratory capability study, and prompt context level is the varied factor. Code-quality results per prompt type appear only in Figure 5, and no numeric values are given in the text. SLOC and Halstead volume showed no appreciable difference across prompt types. Table IV (test pass rates) is garbled in the extraction. The model is named inconsistently: DeepSeek-V2.5 in Table I but DeepSeek-Coder-V2 in the results. A consistency check across multiple generations used CodeBLEU, which is why QA6 is scored partial. Contamination is acknowledged but not mitigated.

extraction.eligibility_reason: This is an LLM multi-agent system that generates Vivado TCL scripts for SoC design. Based on the abstract, the main outcome is pass rate (correctness), and FPGA resource utilization is a hardware-design property rather than an NF quality of the generated code. Only the abstract was available, so this is borderline.

extraction.notes: Decided from the abstract only. Check the full text for whether FPGA resource utilization is treated as an efficiency target of the generated TCL designs. If it is, the paper could qualify as an efficiency outcome for a multi-agent technique.

extraction.eligibility_reason: The abstract describes a comparative evaluation of five LLMs generating Flask CRUD apps, scored with static analysis tools (code health, security). Contamination was handled by filtering synthetic data with more than 75% token overlap with benchmark prompts. Artifact repository was announced as 'will be available'. A secondary result shows CodeQL report plus hint raises the GPT-4 repair rate to 83.99% on average.

extraction.eligibility_reason: Proposes MARCO, a multi-agent loop in which a performance-evaluator agent and web-search retrieval feed back into an LLM optimizer. It reports runtime and memory of the LLM-generated code on LeetCode problems.

techniques.technique_name: MARCO (code optimizer agent + performance evaluator agent + Tavily web search)
techniques.tools: Tavily search API; tracemalloc; psutil 5.9.8; high-resolution timers
techniques.iterations: iterates until convergence or user-defined stopping criteria; max rounds not specified
techniques.metrics: efficiency: average runtime in ms (execution), peak memory in MB (execution via tracemalloc/psutil); correctness: LeetCode submission tests (execution)
techniques.benchmarks: LeetCode 75 (75 easy/medium problems) + 10 randomly selected LeetCode hard problems
techniques.models: Claude 3.5 Sonnet (closed, instruct); GPT-4o (closed, instruct); DeepSeek Coder-V2 (open, code-specialized; baseline only); Llama 3.1 8B (open, instruct; baseline only)
techniques.baselines: Standalone Claude 3.5 Sonnet, GPT-4o, DeepSeek Coder-V2, Llama 3.1 8B; MARCO without web search
techniques.effect_target_headline: average runtime reduction of 14.6% (mean runtime 49.1 ms vs. 57.5 ms) on LeetCode 75 vs Claude-3.5 Sonnet; 51.9% on hard problems; 30.9% improvement over base MARCO without web search

extraction.notes: Correctness is said to be validated via LeetCode submissions, but no correctness results are reported. Readability is only claimed to be preserved and is not measured. It is unclear which LLM backs MARCO for each reported result. Runs were repeated 5 times, but standard deviations are not shown. Memory results are mixed (average 1.2% reduction). The paper has no explicit threats-to-validity section; only limitations are discussed.

extraction.eligibility_reason: Judged from the abstract only. AGCEF appears to be a pre-deployment detection and gating framework for AI-generated IaC and CI/CD configs. Its reported outcomes are detection performance (vulnerability prevention, false negatives, manual review), not an intervention that changes the code the LLM produces. This is borderline, since blocking insecure configurations could count as a post-generation guardrail.
extraction.title: Securing AI-Assisted Cloud Engineering: Guardrails For Copilot-Generated IaC And CI/CD Changes To Prevent Vulnerability Injection
extraction.venue: International Journal of Scientific Research and Engineering Trends
extraction.notes: Only the abstract was available. A reviewer should check the full text for three things: (1) whether AGCEF feeds its findings back to the LLM to regenerate or repair configs, which would make it a post-generation security loop and likely an include; (2) whether security metrics are reported for the resulting generated IaC; (3) whether real experiments were run, given that the venue may have limited peer review.

extraction.eligibility_reason: Proposes an LLM inference framework for generating PDE solver code (CoT, self-debugging, nRMSE-feedback refinement, best-of-n) and reports execution time of the generated solvers. This is borderline: runtime is reported only descriptively per model and PDE, not compared across technique conditions.
extraction.title: CodePDE: An Inference Framework for LLM-driven PDE Solver Generation

techniques.models: 16 LLMs incl. GPT-4o, GPT-4o mini, GPT-4.1, o1-mini, o3, o3-mini, o4-mini (closed); Claude-3.5-haiku, Claude-3.7-sonnet (closed); Gemini 2.0 Flash, 2.0 Flash Thinking, 2.5 Pro (closed); Qwen-2.5-Max, QwQ-Plus; DeepSeek-V3, DeepSeek-R1 (open)
techniques.baselines: Ablations without refine/scale/debug; reference numerical solvers; Dedalus; py-pde; neural solvers (FNO, U-Net, PINN, ORCA, PDEformer, UPS); FunSearch; AIDE

extraction.notes: Borderline IC3. Efficiency (runtime) is reported only per model and PDE in Figs 11 and 13, with no before/after comparison across techniques. The exception is Table 10 (human hint): runtime 191.61s without hint vs 1221.57s with hint, i.e. slower. The refinement prompt explicitly asks for faster code. Figures are garbled in the extracted text.

extraction.eligibility_reason: Proposes an RL fine-tuning technique (RRHF with unit-test and runtime rewards) for CodeT5 so that it generates optimized programs. It reports quantitative runtime efficiency outcomes (%OPT, speedup, runtime reduction) on PIE Python.

extraction.notes: Only one model (CodeT5 60M) is evaluated. Baseline numbers for CodeGen/Codex are copied from the PIE paper, so the comparison is not head-to-head. Pass rate is shown only in a figure (Fig. 2), with no reported number. Energy/power figures describe model training, not the generated code. Timing is the mean of 3 runs. The 30-hour training time is the only compute reported. No threats-to-validity section.

extraction.eligibility_reason: Proposes an MCTS-based agentic workflow search for LLM Verilog generation, with population objectives for area, power and timing. Yosys-synthesized area/power/timing of the generated code is reported quantitatively against baselines; this is treated as efficiency.

techniques.technique_name: VFlow (CEPE-MCTS multi-population agentic workflow search)
techniques.tools: Icarus Verilog (simulation); Yosys (synthesis metrics)

techniques.metrics: efficiency: area (µm2), power (µW), timing slack (ns) via Yosys synthesis [tool-static]; cost: tokens/API cost

techniques.effect_target_headline: adder_16bit area/power: VFlow 126/69 vs IO 157/91 (designer 128/68)
techniques.effect_correctness_headline: VerilogEval-human pass@1 82.8% vs IO 46.6% (+36.1%)

extraction.notes: Verilog hardware design. Area/power/timing are synthesized-circuit properties, mapped here to the efficiency dimension; the reviewer should check this fits the review scope. Table I is garbled: values are repeated across columns and only 9 modules are shown. In the timing column, VFlow's slack is more negative than IO's in several modules (e.g., adder_16bit -1.20 vs -0.33), so the timing direction is unclear and the overall efficiency effect may be mixed. Sections report inconsistent improvement figures (Table II row vs text +19.6%/+30.9%). Parameter values (θ, λ, β, weights) are not given.

Reviewer should decide whether this paper belongs in the 'context' side list instead. Most metric differences are not statistically significant (Wilcoxon test, Holm correction); only Pylint Warning and PMD Code Style differ significantly, with negligible-to-small effect sizes. Contamination is handled only partially: 8 McEval Python tasks overlapping with HumanEval were removed. Extracted tables are garbled.

extraction.eligibility_reason: Based on the abstract only, this is a benchmark/evaluation framework measuring the correctness and ReDoS security (vulnerable@k) of LLM-generated regexes. extraction.notes: Decided from the abstract only. Borderline: the full text should be checked for whether raw prompts and refined prompts (with examples) are compared on vulnerable@k. If they are, this could count as a prompting intervention with a security outcome, which would change the decision to include.

extraction.eligibility_reason: Neither the full text nor an abstract is available. extraction.eligibility_reason: SynthCoder is a training technique (anti-pattern-aware masking, SFT and DPO) for LLM FIM code completion, but its outcomes are correctness or similarity metrics (EM, ES, Pass@1) plus code-echo ratio and generated-token length. These are inference-cost and usability measures, not readability, maintainability, runtime/memory efficiency or security of the generated code.

extraction.notes: Borderline case. Mean generation length is called 'efficiency' by the authors, but it measures inference tokens, not the runtime efficiency of the generated code. Code-echo ratio is an erroneous-repetition defect rate, not an NF quality dimension as defined for this review.

extraction.eligibility_reason: The paper evaluates RAG with retrieved similar solved LeetCode problems as a technique for LLM code generation. It reports quantitative efficiency outcomes (runtime and memory percentile vs. other submissions from the LeetCode judge) for the generated code.

extraction.venue: Proceedings of the 40th Brazilian Symposium on Data Bases (SBBD)

techniques.benchmarks: 30 LeetCode test problems (5 Easy, 19 Medium, 6 Hard); knowledge base of 120 LeetCode problems
techniques.models: GPT-4o (closed, general); Claude 3.7 Sonnet (closed); GPT-3.5 Turbo (closed); Gemini 2.0 Flash (closed); Qwen2.5-Coder-32B (open, code-specialized); DeepSeek-R1 (open, reasoning)

extraction.notes: Short paper (pp. 851-857), so IC4 should be verified. The efficiency metric is LeetCode's percentile-beaten score, which is noisy and was taken from single runs. The baseline does not control for prompt length; the authors acknowledge this. Test problems were selected so that at least one similar problem is retrieved. Contamination is addressed only partially, by reporting results for 2023-2025 problems. Table 2 is somewhat garbled in the extraction. Exact adaptive threshold values above and below the 65% minimum are not given.

extraction.eligibility_reason: An off-the-shelf LLM iteratively proposes loop-transformation schedules that are applied to existing PolyBench code, guided by compiler legality and measured-speedup feedback. Runtime speedup of the resulting optimized code is reported. This is borderline because the LLM emits transformation commands and the compiler generates the code; an ablation (RQ7) has the LLM rewrite the C code directly.

extraction.venue: 2025 34th International Conference on Parallel Architectures and Compilation Techniques (PACT)

techniques.iterations: T=30 iterations (distinct schedules) per run; LLM may issue no_further_transformations but is pushed to continue up to the iteration limit; best-of-K=5 runs
techniques.metrics: efficiency: geometric mean of median speedup over the original code, Pluto and the Tiramisu autoscheduler [execution]; correctness: legality guaranteed by dependence analysis, plus runnable/invalid/illegal schedule rates; output comparison in the RQ7 direct-code-generation variant
techniques.benchmarks: PolyBench/C 4.2.1, 30 kernels x 5 dataset sizes = 150 instances
techniques.models: gemini-2.0-flash (closed); gpt-4o (closed); gpt-o3-mini (closed, reasoning); gemma3 27B (open); llama3.3 70B (open, instruct); qwq 32B (open, reasoning); qwen2.5-coder 32B (open, code); codestral-2501 22B (open, code)
techniques.baselines: original code; Pluto polyhedral optimizer; Tiramisu deep-learning autoscheduler; no-feedback ablation; LLM direct code generation variant
techniques.effect_target_headline: geometric mean speedups of 2.66x (single run) and 3.54x (best-of-5 runs) over the original code; 2.94× over Pluto (best-of-5)
techniques.effect_correctness_headline: 36.1% of the proposed schedules are successfully compiled and run (runnable), while 31.4% are invalid and 32.5% are illegal

extraction.notes: Borderline on IC2/EC4: the LLM selects transformation commands rather than writing code, and the code being optimized is human-written PolyBench. Contamination is only partly addressed: identifiers are anonymized for robustness, not for contamination. There is no explicit threats-to-validity section. Some figures are garbled in the extracted text.

extraction.eligibility_reason: Proposes an LLM-driven evolutionary framework (GPT-4o-mini) that generates optimized RTL variants, and reports quantitative power, area and delay (efficiency) of the LLM-produced code, with correctness as a co-outcome. Borderline because the inputs are human-written designs being optimized, but the evaluated artifact is new code generated by the LLM.

The paper states equal numbers of LLM calls across methods but gives no counts. Single run and single model. Table 1 is garbled in the extraction. Ablation results are reported as best-counts only. Prompts are not provided and the UCB exploration coefficient c is not given.

extraction.eligibility_reason: The paper benchmarks 11 open LLMs prompted with a single fixed few-shot prompt to derive GPU thread-mapping functions. Runtime and energy of the generated kernels are reported only against a naive bounding-box baseline and human-derived equations, not against an LLM generating without the technique, so no intervention to improve the NF quality of LLM code is evaluated. Eligibility is borderline.
extraction.title: Leveraging Mathematical Reasoning of LLMs for Efficient GPU Thread Mapping
extraction.notes: Borderline case. The paper frames LLM use as an efficiency technique: the generated kernels give up to 4833x speedup and 2890x energy reduction. That baseline, however, is a naive bounding-box mapping, not an LLM without the technique. Context size (20/50/100 points) is varied, but it is reported mainly for correctness and for inference energy, not for the efficiency of the generated code. A reviewer could argue for inclusion as a prompting technique with efficiency outcomes. The GPU timing results come from CUDA kernels into which the LLM-derived logic was integrated; the models themselves generated Python functions.

extraction.eligibility_reason: Proposes a multi-agent LLM framework that generates Verilog RTL code, and reports quantitative PPA outcomes (power/energy, latency, area) of the generated hardware as an efficiency dimension. It is borderline because PPA is a hardware-design efficiency measure rather than software runtime efficiency, and it is compared only against a human-expert design.

extraction.venue: 2025 IEEE/ACM International Conference On Computer Aided Design (ICCAD)

Baseline LLMs fail completely (Pass@5 = 0), so PPA is compared only against the CLARIE human-expert design, with mixed results. Table III is garbled. Thresholds t_sim, t_w and beta are not reported. Human-written debugging manuals are used after C rounds, and testbenches are written manually with LLM assistance.

extraction.eligibility_reason: Empirically evaluates seven PEFT methods (training-time interventions) on eight code LLMs, measuring the security of the generated code (static-analysis secure rate). HumanEval pass@k is reported as the correctness co-outcome.

techniques.metrics: security: Compilation-Rate, Secure-Rate, Overall-Secure-Rate [tool-static], expert review of 300 samples [human]; poisoning: vulnerability counts under TrojanPuzzle [tool-static]; maintainability: CC, MI, LOC, HV via Radon [tool-static], comparing prompt-tuned output with human code only
techniques.benchmarks: LLMSecEval subset (81 prompts, 13 CWEs, x6 temperatures = 486 samples per configuration); HumanEval; TrojanPuzzle poisoning (36 prompts); AixBench Java (186 prompts)

techniques.baselines: Base model without fine-tuning; SVEN
techniques.effect_target_headline: prompt-tuning achieving an 80.86% Overall-Secure-Rate on CodeGen2 16B, a 13.5-point improvement over the 67.28% baseline
techniques.effect_correctness_headline: CodeLlama 7B prompt-tuning pass@1 37.89% vs 35.09% baseline

extraction.human_eval_details: 3 security experts rated 300 snippets as secure/insecure; Fleiss' kappa 0.791 (binary classification) and 0.612 (qualitative assessment); 87.3% agreement with automated tools
extraction.notes: Several internal inconsistencies: Takeaway 1 claims a 20.4%p gain on CodeGen2 16B, while the headline says 13.5 (13.58 per Table 2); the paper says it compares prompt-tuning against SVEN on CodeGen2 7B using 73.66 vs 72.43, but those are Compilation-Rates; one cell reads 336/322; only two of the three tools are named in the Section 5.1 text. Temperature results also act as a decoding variable. Radon metrics are a human-vs-LLM comparison only, not a before/after technique effect, so the readability-maintainability effect is recorded as NR. Many appendix statistics may be unverifiable. Contamination is marked partial because only train/eval leakage via similarity deduplication is addressed. No artifact URL is given.

extraction.eligibility_reason: Proposes PROD, a training-time unlearning technique applied to code LLMs, and evaluates the security of the generated code completions with CyberSecEval's static analyzer pass rate (combined with 1-BLEU), alongside HumanEval correctness.
extraction.title: Large Language Model Unlearning for Source Code

techniques.technique_name: PROD (Probabilistic Redistribution for Output Distribution) unlearning
techniques.tools: CyberSecEval built-in static analyzer (Insecure Code Detector)
techniques.metrics: security: forget quality = average of (1-BLEU vs vulnerable snippet [similarity-to-reference]) and CyberSecEval static analyzer pass rate [tool-static]; combined with utility via Pareto Dominance Ratio (PDR); human/GPT-4 pairwise perceptual win rate [human, llm-judge]
techniques.benchmarks: CyberSecEval (Purple Llama) insecure code autocomplete, 1,916 snippets, 50 CWEs; also copyrighted code (100 Stack files) and deprecated API (VersiCode-derived, 3,449 snippets); HumanEval for utility
techniques.models: CodeLlama-7B, open, code-specialized; Qwen2.5-Coder-7B, open, code-specialized; DeepSeek-Coder-6.7B, open, code-specialized; StarCoder-7B, open, code-specialized
techniques.baselines: Gradient Ascent, DPO, NPO, FLAT; original model
techniques.effect_target_headline: Insecurity PDR: Ours 70.4 vs NPO 24.5 (CodeLlama-7B)

extraction.human_eval_details: 3 evaluators with at least 2 years of development experience; 20 samples per task; pairwise win rate; no agreement statistic reported
extraction.notes: Security is one of three unlearning tasks. The forget metric mixes BLEU with static-analyzer pass rate, and the security results are reported mainly as PDR and plots, not as raw vulnerability rates. Only CodeLlama-7B was used for the security task; the other three models were tested on the copyright task only. Utility (HumanEval) is lower than the original model, so the correctness effect is a decline relative to no unlearning but better than the baselines. Results are averaged over 5 seeds but no variance is reported for the main results. The model was first fine-tuned on the forget data. Borderline fit to the review topic: removing memorized insecure snippets.

extraction.eligibility_reason: The abstract describes fine-tuning LLMs on security-vetted, domain-specific datasets and reports that the fine-tuned models generate more secure, regulation-compliant code than general-purpose LLMs. This appears to satisfy IC1–IC3, but the decision rests on the abstract only.

extraction.eligibility_reason: From the abstract alone, TACO is an evaluation and trust-assessment framework with benchmarks for LLM responses in coding assistance. It does not propose or evaluate a technique that changes the code an LLM generates; it assesses code quality and intent alignment across models.

extraction.venue: Proceedings of the 2026 IEEE/ACM 48th International Conference on Software Engineering
extraction.notes: Decision based on the abstract only. It is a benchmark/evaluator paper (LLM-as-judge for code quality plus intent alignment) and likely belongs on the context list. Check the full text in case TACO is used as a feedback signal to improve generation.

extraction.eligibility_reason: No full text or abstract is available. The title describes a multi-agent code generation framework focused on resilience and budget, and gives no evidence that any quantitative non-functional quality outcome is reported.
extraction.title: FTDI: A Budget-Aware Self-Healing Framework for Resilient LLM Multi-Agent Code Generation
extraction.notes: Only the title was available; there was no abstract or full text. This is an SSRN preprint. The 'resilience' and 'self-healing' framing may refer to fault tolerance of the agents rather than to the quality of the generated code. The side-list assignment (correctness-only) is a guess from the title alone. A reviewer should retrieve the full text to check for NF metrics such as efficiency or cost of the generated code.

Whether a quantitative NF outcome is reported cannot be verified without the full text, so inclusion is provisional and borderline.

extraction.eligibility_reason: Based on the abstract only, the paper studies how different prompt inputs affect LLM repair of existing human-written vulnerable code. This is vulnerability repair of human code, and the outcome reported is repair accuracy (patch correctness) rather than an NF quality measure of newly generated code.
extraction.title: Not All Input Helps: What Information Should We Feed to LLMs for Vulnerability Repair?
extraction.notes: Abstract only. Check whether the full text measures security of the repaired code (e.g., vulnerability removal verified by a tool). Even so, the paper is likely adjacent (EC4: repair of human-written code). Also check the page count, since NIER papers are short (4 pages); IC4 might be borderline.

extraction.eligibility_reason: This is a thesis on migrating existing monolithic (human-written) systems to microservices. LLM-guided packaging transforms existing code, which makes it adjacent refactoring work. From the abstract alone, there is no clear quantitative NF outcome on LLM-generated code from an intervention.
extraction.title: A machine learning-based framework to support monoliths to microservices migration: from identification to packaging and deployment
extraction.notes: Decided from the abstract only. MicroPacker (LLM-guided modularisation) might report modularity or architecture-quality metrics on LLM-transformed code. A reviewer should check the full thesis or the related papers. The thesis also includes an SLR, which is a secondary component, and generates Kubernetes and Docker configs via RAG, which may not count as production code.

extraction.eligibility_reason: The title points to a prompt-engineering technique for reducing vulnerabilities in LLM-generated code across several models and languages, which would satisfy IC1-IC3 for the security dimension. Neither the full text nor an abstract was available, so eligibility is provisional and must be verified.
extraction.title: Securing LLM code generation: Leveraging prompt engineering to mitigate vulnerabilities across models and languages

Also confirm the study type: it is unclear whether this is a technique-proposal or a technique-evaluation.

extraction.eligibility_reason: The paper proposes an LLM agent that writes Manim code to render educational videos. Its outcomes are video aesthetics, knowledge transfer, and pipeline generation time and token cost. None of these is a non-functional quality measure of the generated code itself (readability, runtime/memory efficiency of the code, or security).

extraction.notes: 'Code efficiency' in this paper means generation latency and token consumption of the pipeline, not the runtime efficiency of the generated code. A reviewer may want to confirm this borderline reading.

extraction.eligibility_reason: PSSec (SFT+RL on lightweight Qwen3 models) is evaluated only on analysing and repairing existing human-written PowerShell scripts from The Stack, measuring static-analyzer fix success. The CodeGen part of the benchmark measures security of LLM-generated scripts without any intervention, which is context only.
extraction.title: Lightweight Yet Secure: Secure Scripting Language Generation via Lightweight LLMs
extraction.notes: Borderline case. IC2 allows code edited by an LLM, and the paper frames PSSec as a downstream fixer for code produced by a frontier LLM. However, every reported PSSec result is on repair of human-written scripts from The Stack. The NF metric is FSucRate: PSScriptAnalyzer Warning/Error-level violations removed. Many of the rules are style or readability rules rather than security rules. A reviewer should decide whether LLM repair of existing code satisfies IC2; if so, the paper should be included under security with a training-time technique.

extraction.eligibility_reason: Nettle uses LLMs with compiler/test feedback to repair human-written Codeforces submissions that hit Time Limit Exceeded errors, which is LLM repair of human-written code. Its outcomes are repair (pass) rate under a time limit and edit distance; no separate quantitative efficiency metric such as runtime or speedup is reported.
extraction.title: A Systematic Study of Time Limit Exceeded Errors in Online Programming Assignments
extraction.notes: Borderline case. The LLM does edit the code, and passing within the time limit is partly an efficiency outcome. However, the evaluated artifact is a repair of human-written code, and success is a binary pass/fail verdict that mixes correctness with the time limit; no runtime numbers are reported. A reviewer may judge that this falls under IC2/IC3 as LLM-edited code with an efficiency outcome.

extraction.eligibility_reason: Proposes a multi-agent, EDA-tool-integrated framework with evolving memory for LLM Verilog generation, and reports quantitative PPA metrics (delay, area, power; an efficiency dimension) for the generated code, alongside pass@k correctness.

extraction.notes: The output is hardware RTL (Verilog), so PPA is treated as efficiency; this mapping is borderline, and the reviewer should check scope. Many designs are N/A (no functionally correct, synthesizable design), so the geometric mean may be computed over different design subsets. No variance or repeated runs, no compute reporting, and no threats-to-validity section. The ablation lists 'w/o PPA Analyzer' in Table 3 but describes it as 'w/o PPA Agent' in the text.

extraction.eligibility_reason: The abstract describes an LLM technique, BinDec, that alternates LLM decompilation with symbolic-execution verification to produce source code. It reports significantly improved readability (an NF dimension) alongside semantic accuracy. extraction.eligibility_reason: The specialist BPMN-to-ReAct-agent pipeline is an LLM code-generation technique, but its outcomes are essentially functional: tool-use exactness, process adherence, tool-call errors and repair iterations, plus generation token cost. The only runtime-like metric is penalty-adjusted latency, which mixes the generated agent's execution time with correctness penalties. Maintainability is claimed but never measured. Borderline exclusion.
extraction.title: Beyond Generalist LLMs: Specialist Agentic Systems for Structured Code Workflow Execution
extraction.notes: Borderline. Penalty-adjusted latency (2.49 s per effective step vs 6.59 for Cline and 9.08 for Roo) is defined as T/P, where P is correct tool calls minus missed, excess and out-of-sequence calls. It therefore measures the runtime of the generated agent, which is dominated by LLM calls, combined with correctness penalties; it is not a pure code-efficiency metric. A reviewer could reasonably treat it as an efficiency outcome and include the paper. If included: the technique is a hybrid template/structured pipeline with execution-based self-refinement; baselines are Roo and Cline; the backend LLM is not named; the judge is GPT-4.1; there is no artifact URL. Generation token cost refers to the generator's cost, not to a property of the generated code. Repair iterations and the coefficient of variation are also reported.

extraction.eligibility_reason: The paper proposes a defense against prompt injection in inter-agent messages of multi-agent LLM systems. Its outcome is attack success rate and blocking of unauthorized effects induced by adversarial messages, which is robustness to attack rather than the vulnerability or security quality of generated code in the CWE sense.

extraction.notes: Borderline case. The code ASR metric measures whether released generated code performs unauthorized effects such as exfiltration. A reviewer could treat this as the security of LLM-generated code; if so, it would be an include as a post-generation-loop technique: release boundary with an EffectIR static checker plus clean-room regeneration, at most 2 generations. Evaluation details: HumanEval (164 tasks) and MBPP (500 tasks); models Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct, Qwen3.5-9B and Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.2; ESC-CR code ASR reported as 0.00 in most cells. The paper refers to an appendix that is not included in the text. No artifact URL is given.

extraction.eligibility_reason: Judging from the abstract, this thesis contributes a benchmark (CodeEval) and a code-quality assessment model (CodeQualBERT). It does not propose any technique that changes LLM-generated code to improve its non-functional quality. It evaluates and assesses LLM code but does not intervene in how that code is produced.

extraction.notes: Decision based on the abstract only; the full text was not available. The work appears to be a thesis. CodeQual scores code quality along dimensions such as readability and efficiency, but its samples come from existing sources rather than from an intervention on LLM generation. Check the full text for whether any part uses the quality model as feedback to improve generation.

extraction.notes: This is an empirical study of security regression within a feedback loop, not a technique proposal. It is included because the loop's per-iteration security trajectory and the comparison of prompting strategies are quantitative NF outcomes. Model attribution is missing for the non-RAG runs, so prompting-strategy comparisons are confounded with model mix. Each configuration was run once, so run-to-run variance is unquantified; statistical tests are reported. Syntax validity is tracked, but its rate is not reported as a headline number. Reviewers may want to check whether this paper belongs in the context side list, since it measures the security effect of an existing loop rather than proposing an improvement.

extraction.eligibility_reason: The paper trains a VLM critic that detects UI principle violations in pages that had violations synthetically injected. extraction.eligibility_reason: The paper trains and benchmarks reward models that score code preference pairs, which are mostly human-written GitHub commits and contest solutions. The outcome is RM preference accuracy, not the NF quality of code that an LLM generated or edited under an intervention. No downstream policy training or best-of-n generation is evaluated for NF quality; the only re-ranking experiment measures correctness.
extraction.title: Themis: Training Robust Multilingual Code Reward Models for Flexible Multi-Criteria Scoring
extraction.notes: The paper is a reward-model and benchmark contribution. The listwise re-ranking experiment on CodeContests+ uses LLM-generated solutions but measures only correctness (Hits@10, rank correlation). NF dimensions appear only as RM preference accuracy. The paper could be reconsidered if the review treats reward-model evaluation as in scope.

extraction.eligibility_reason: The paper fine-tunes an LLM and adds a verification pipeline for P4 code generation, but the abstract reports only compilation rate and solution success. These are correctness/compilability outcomes. The pipeline mentions 'runtime performance validation', but the abstract gives no quantitative non-functional outcome.
extraction.title: PINC (P4 and Intent for Network Configuration): A Prototype Using Large Language Models
extraction.notes: Decision is based on the abstract only. The verification pipeline includes 'runtime performance validation', so the full text may report efficiency metrics for the generated P4 code (e.g., throughput or latency). Check the full text before finalizing; if such metrics are reported, this paper could become an include.

extraction.eligibility_reason: The paper evaluates LLM-generated native Android UI code and compares plain prompts with prompts that ask for accessibility. Its only quality outcome is UI accessibility (Accessibility Scanner error counts), which is not one of the review's NF dimensions (readability-maintainability, efficiency, security). The study is mainly an empirical characterization rather than a technique proposal.
extraction.title: Designing for all? Accessibility of native android interfaces from large language models
extraction.venue: Universal Access in the Information Society
extraction.notes: Borderline. If the review's NF scope is extended to accessibility or usability, reconsider inclusion. The paper does test an intervention: an 'AccessReq' follow-up prompt ('Rewrite the screen code to make it accessible'). Across all studies this prompt increased errors (387 vs 315; paired t = -2.739, p = 0.00694). Other variables tested were layout framework and prompt language. Studies 1-2 overlap with the earlier MOBILESoft 2025 paper (ref [14]); check for duplication. The full text is a Research Square preprint of the version published in UAIS.

extraction.eligibility_reason: Based on the abstract only, this thesis evaluates LLM repair of existing human-written vulnerable code from CrossVul, comparing outputs to ground-truth fixes with similarity metrics (CodeBLEU, AST edit distance, ROUGE). That is LLM repair of human-written code rather than improving the NF quality of LLM-generated code.
extraction.title: Exploring LLM Performance For Vulnerability Mitigation
extraction.venue: Gothenburg University Publications Electronic Archive (Gothenburg University)
extraction.notes: Only the abstract was available. This is a thesis (likely a master's thesis), so it may not meet IC4 as a peer-reviewed paper or preprint. It compares four prompt styles for vulnerability repair, which makes it borderline: the security outcome is measured only by similarity to reference fixes plus manual analysis. Check the full text to see whether any security metric, such as a static analyzer, is applied to the LLM-produced fixes.

extraction.eligibility_reason: The paper evaluates two prompting interventions, self-refinement and RAG, on open-source LLMs and reports quantitative crate hallucination rate (CHR) in generated Rust code. The paper frames this as a supply-chain security risk. Eligibility is borderline because CHR may instead be read as a correctness/reliability measure.

The authors note CHR is a source-level indicator, not direct security evidence, so a reviewer could instead classify this as correctness-only. Most of the paper is empirical characterization (RQ1–RQ2); mitigation is only RQ3, and statistical tests are reported only for RQ1, not for the mitigation results. Code quality/correctness was not measured despite the abstract's claim of 'without sacrificing code quality'.

extraction.eligibility_reason: KEET is a multi-agent LLM framework that turns Nsight Compute profiles into performance explanations. These explanations are fed as context to an LLM that optimizes CUDA kernels, and the paper reports speedup@1 (efficiency) and pass@1 for the LLM-edited code.

techniques.effect_correctness_headline: average pass@1: KEET 0.77, KEET+DrGPU 0.78, Code-based 0.74, DrGPU 0.77

extraction.notes: KEET's primary output is explanations, but the evaluation measures speedup of LLM-optimized code that uses those explanations as context, so the technique is categorized as a pre-generation context intervention. Figures are garbled; speedups are mostly read from plots. Table III shows best-attempt speedups (e.g., gaussian 14.0 vs 12.4). Failed attempts are excluded from speedup@1. No threats-to-validity section and no artifacts are provided.

extraction.eligibility_reason: This is a book chapter that discusses generative AI within the Secure Software Development Life Cycle and DevSecOps case studies. It mentions prompt engineering as a mitigation, but the abstract reports no empirical evaluation of a technique and no quantitative security outcome for LLM-generated code; it reads as a conceptual or overview chapter.
extraction.title: Secure Code Generation and Software Engineering With Generative AI
extraction.venue: Advances in computational intelligence and robotics book series
extraction.notes: Only the abstract was available. This is a book chapter and possibly a discursive or secondary-style piece (EC2 may also apply). The case studies may contain empirical data; check the full text if obtainable.

extraction.eligibility_reason: The paper proposes GRPO fine-tuning of an LLM (Qwen2.5-Coder-7B) with a programmatic rubric reward to generate OpenQASM/Qiskit circuit code. Inclusion is borderline because T-count is a quantum-resource metric rather than classical runtime or memory.

extraction.eligibility_reason: This RL technique for LLM website generation targets functional success, rendering validity and VLM-judged visual aesthetics of the rendered UI; none of these is a code-level NF dimension (readability-maintainability, efficiency, security). The only code-level static metric, LDPR (ESLint plus dependency resolution pass rate), appears only in a group-size ablation figure, with no values in the text and no comparison against the base model or baselines.
extraction.title: WebGen-R1: Incentivizing Large Language Models to Generate Functional and Aesthetic Websites with Reinforcement Learning
extraction.notes: Borderline exclusion. A reviewer should decide two points: (1) whether the ESLint-based LDPR, shown only in Figure 5 for the GRPO group-size ablation, counts as a readability-maintainability outcome; (2) whether visual aesthetics of the rendered website (AAS, VLM-judged with GPT-4o) is in scope for the review. If either is accepted, the paper would be a training-time technique: SFT warm-up plus GRPO on Qwen2.5-Coder-7B-Instruct, evaluated on WebGen-Bench (101 tasks) and a 119-task WebDev Arena subset. Code and data: https://github.com/juyongjiang/WebGen-R1.

extraction.eligibility_reason: The multi-agent framework (RAG plus static analysis plus agents) is evaluated only on code correctness, debugging accuracy, documentation BLEU, latency, satisfaction and time saved. extraction.notes: The PyLint/ESLint flag rate of 12.3% is reported only in the Discussion, as 'preliminary', and has no comparison. Response latency is a tool metric, not the efficiency of the generated code. Low-rigor venue; the reported numbers look unverifiable.

extraction.eligibility_reason: The abstract describes a framework for selecting LLMs and prompting configurations to improve the syntactic validity and general 'quality' of code in niche languages such as OCL. extraction.eligibility_reason: AutoGate uses LLM agents to rewrite existing human-written RTL (Verilog) designs so that synthesis can infer clock gating, measuring circuit dynamic power. extraction.notes: Borderline case. The LLM edits code (IC2 could arguably hold), and the outcome is hardware dynamic power, which might be read as efficiency. The input is existing human-written RTL, so the paper was classed as adjacent (LLM refactoring). A reviewer should confirm how the review treats LLM-based RTL power optimization.

extraction.eligibility_reason: Proposes a pre-generation, activation-based predictor of CSS/MI used for model selection (routing) among LLMs, which changes which LLM-generated code is delivered. Its effect on the maintainability of the selected code is measured quantitatively (MRQS from Pylint and radon). Eligibility is borderline: the technique is a selector or router rather than a change to any single model's output.

extraction.eligibility_reason: The paper proposes an LLM tool-making pipeline that generates, tests and repairs code tools, but the generated code is evaluated only by pass@1 and end-to-end accuracy. extraction.eligibility_reason: Abstract describes an RL-based training strategy that improves LLM C code generation, evaluated with a memory-safety metric (MSC), which is a security NF outcome. Only the abstract was available, IEEE DataPort is a dataset venue, and full-paper status (IC4) is uncertain.
extraction.title: CForge

techniques.metrics: security: Memory Safety of C (MSC), a newly proposed metric targeting memory leaks and buffer overflows (instrument type unclear from abstract)
techniques.benchmarks: CForge (6000+ C programming tasks)

extraction.notes: Only the abstract was available. Verify that this is a full paper and not only a dataset entry on IEEE DataPort, since IC4 is uncertain. The abstract gives no results for the RL strategy, so effects are NR. The reward signal source is assumed from the RL framing and is likely MSC-based; check how MSC is measured (e.g., a sanitizer such as Valgrind or ASan would be execution-based). Fill in models and baselines from the full text.

extraction.eligibility_reason: CROCODIL is a GRPO post-training technique that applies to LLM edits of LLM-generated Rust code, but its target outcome is edit size (Levenshtein distance from the pre-edit code). That measures edit minimality rather than the readability, efficiency or security of the resulting code. Apart from edit size, only build and test success are reported. Borderline, since minimal edits could be argued to support maintainability and reviewability.
extraction.title: CROCODIL: Cross-Model Code Editing with LLMs
extraction.notes: Human reviewer should decide whether excessive-edit reduction (edit distance) counts as a readability-maintainability outcome. The strict-prompt guidelines mention preserving naming and style, but no style or quality metric is measured. If included: family training, GRPO with a similarity × execution reward on Olmo3 7B with LoRA; effect on edit size is +, with the All-tasks normalized char distance at roughly half the base model's (e.g. 0.54 to 0.20 on Qwen3.5 35B A3B implementations); correctness is mostly +. Artifacts are at https://github.com/EngineeringSoftware/Crocodil.

extraction.eligibility_reason: Proposes JevVibe, a diagnosis-guided repair agent. It repairs code generated by Qwen2.5-Coder-32B-Instruct using a predicted CWE label and reports the security pass rate measured by CyberSecEval's Insecure Code Detector.
extraction.title: JevVibe: Efficient Classification-Guided Secure Code Generation

techniques.technique_name: JevVibe: CWE classification-guided repair (Jev typed-choice diagnosis + LLM repair)
techniques.tools: Jev-1.13.0 (TypeSafe AI) typed Choice classifier; vLLM; CyberSecEval Insecure Code Detector used for evaluation only
techniques.iterations: single repair round using the Top-1 CWE; falls back to the original code if diagnosis or repair fails
techniques.metrics: security: security pass rate, fix rate, regression rate and net fixes, all measured with the CyberSecEval Insecure Code Detector [tool-static]
techniques.benchmarks: CyberSecEval Instruct (PurpleLlama), 1,916 tasks
techniques.languages: C, C++, C#, Java, JavaScript, PHP, Python, Rust
techniques.models: Qwen2.5-Coder-32B-Instruct (open, code-specialized) as generator and repairer; Jev-1.13.0 (closed decision model) as classifier
techniques.baselines: unrepaired baseline; LLM-guided repair using Qwen2.5-Coder-32B-Instruct's own CWE diagnosis
techniques.effect_target_headline: security pass rate from 63.5% before repair to 70.7%, compared with 66.1% for LLM-guided repair

extraction.notes: Functional correctness of the repaired code is not measured. Only one repair model is used. Jev is a proprietary vendor model, which limits reimplementation. Cost and latency are reported only for the classification step. The paper reports regressions alongside fixes: LLM-guided repair regresses 79 baseline-secure examples and Jev-guided repair regresses 89. The classification experiment repurposes the benchmark's origin_code snippets for CWE classification, so it does not itself evaluate generated code.

extraction.eligibility_reason: The paper benchmarks LLMs on detecting and repairing security issues in human-written logging code drawn from real-world issue reports. The repair outcome is measured only as textual similarity to developer patches plus a manual 'effective' judgment, so this is LLM repair of human-written code rather than generation, and no NF security metric is computed on the generated code.
extraction.title: Towards Secure Logging: Characterizing and Benchmarking Logging Code Security Issues with LLMs
extraction.notes: Borderline case. The study compares prompt-context variants (+E, +D, +E+D) for LLM security repair of logging code. However, the edited code is human-written, and repair quality is measured by patch similarity to the developer fix and a manual effectiveness check, not by a security tool. A reviewer could argue for inclusion if repair security outcomes are treated as an NF security dimension. Replication package: https://github.com/defects4log/SecLogging.

extraction.eligibility_reason: This is a Zenodo dataset upload, not a full paper. It describes an LLM-judge evaluation of RAG-specialized agents versus a non-RAG agent, scored on maintainability, security and efficiency, but no paper reporting quantitative results is available.
extraction.title: An Extension to BigCodeBench for Task Characterization and LLM-based Agent Evaluation
extraction.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
extraction.notes: Only the abstract was available. The record is a dataset description; it compares domain-specific RAG agents (Llama-3.1-8B-instruct) against a general no-RAG agent, with GPT-4o-mini judging NF criteria. If an associated paper with results exists, it may be eligible, with RAG as the technique and LLM-judge NF metrics; check for a companion publication.

extraction.eligibility_reason: Proposes energy-aware SFT plus GRPO with simulation reward for LLMs that rewrite inefficient C++ programs, and reports quantitative energy-efficiency outcomes (CARET, ERR, Beat-GT) alongside correctness.
extraction.title: Beyond the Need for Speed: Energy-Aware Code Generation via Simulation-Guided Reinforcement Learning

techniques.tools: Sniper interval simulator + McPAT (AMD EPYC 9554P Zen4 config, 1.5 GHz); g++ -O3 -std=c++17 -static; vLLM; LoRA rank 64
techniques.iterations: GRPO 1 epoch over 15,853 prompts, K=16 rollouts per prompt; SFT 3 epochs

techniques.models: Qwen2.5-Coder-14B (open, base) main; Qwen2.5-Coder-7B and DeepSeek-Coder-6.7B with GRPO; SFT also on Qwen2.5-Coder-0.5B, Llama-3.1-8B, Gemma-3-12B-IT, Gemini-2.5-Flash (closed); zero-shot refs Qwen2.5-Coder-32B, DeepSeek-Coder-V2-Lite

techniques.effect_correctness_headline: compilation rate rises from 60.3% to 81.7%; pass@1 improves from 28.18% to 31.40%, pass@10 regresses from 48.95% to 46.15%

extraction.notes: Energy measured via simulation (Sniper/McPAT), spot-checked against RAPL (93% non-contradiction). Single-seed RL runs; Wilcoxon tests reported. Against Afterburner-style runtime baseline the E-SFT+energy gain is small (12.78 vs 12.19). Contamination argued only informally. Year 2026 arXiv.

extraction.eligibility_reason: The abstract describes a cross-lingual (non-English prompt) code generation technique evaluated on functional quality/correctness benchmarks. No quantitative non-functional outcome is indicated, and the record appears to be an auto-generated synthesis report rather than a full paper.
extraction.title: Cross-lingual Code Generation Performance via Intermediate Python Task Training
extraction.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
extraction.notes: Abstract only and truncated. The text appears to be an autonomous synthesis report ('Assignee Research', 'Tribunal consensus score'), which may also fail IC4. 'Code quality' in the abstract likely refers to correctness (pass@k).

extraction.eligibility_reason: The LLM-generated Python priority functions are judged by the schedule latency they produce on HLS DAGs, which is the quality of the optimization problem's solution, not the code's own non-functional quality. Heuristic runtime is folded into a composite score and is not reported as a code-efficiency outcome against a code baseline, so this is best read as LLM-driven heuristic search for EDA.
extraction.title: RAG-Enhanced Kernel-Based Heuristic Synthesis (RKHS): A Structured Methodology Using Large Language Models for Hardware Design
extraction.notes: Borderline case. A reviewer could argue that the heuristic runtime (Table 1 reports runtime in ms, and the abstract cites 1.3× runtime overhead) counts as an efficiency measure of the generated code. However, that overhead is a cost the technique incurs, not an improvement in the code's efficiency. The paper is short, about 4 pages plus appendix. Only GPT-4 is used, there is no artifact, and there is no code-quality baseline.

extraction.eligibility_reason: The framework feeds static-analysis diagnostics into an iterative LLM loop that refactors existing human-written research notebook code from 10 GitHub repositories. Under the review's protocol, LLM refactoring of human-written code is an adjacent study rather than NF improvement of LLM-generated code.
extraction.title: From Metrics to Improvement: A Lifecycle-Aware LLM Feedback Framework for Research Software Quality
extraction.notes: Borderline case. The LLM-edited code is the evaluated artifact, and maintainability metrics (Pylint, Radon MI/CC, JSCPD duplication, comment density) are reported for iterative feedback vs. single-step vs. unstructured prompting with GPT-4o, GPT-4o-mini, GPT-5-nano and local models. If the reviewer reads IC2 ('edited by an LLM') as covering LLM refactoring of human code, this paper would qualify for inclusion as a feedback-loop technique using static-analyzer signals with a 5-iteration cap. Correctness is not validated; the authors note the absence of tests. Code is available on GitHub (QCDIS/Software_Quality_Control_LLM).

extraction.eligibility_reason: The study fine-tunes BLOOM models on original vs security-sanitized data, a training-time intervention, and reports the percentage of secure code in the generated Java. This meets IC1-IC3. The decision is based on the abstract only.

extraction.eligibility_reason: Proposes a profiler-guided iterative agent loop that has LLMs produce repository-level code edits. It reports quantitative runtime efficiency outcomes (speedup, Opt@1) alongside correctness.

extraction.notes: Results are single-run; the paired win/loss comparison is claimed to be statistically significant, but no test is named. No code URL is given. Hack detection combines an LLM judge with SWE-fficiency's detector. The comparison has confounds: different harnesses (Mini-SWE-Agent vs OpenHands).

extraction.eligibility_reason: SAGE is a diagnostic trace-analysis method that localizes where agentic vulnerability repairs went wrong. It does not change the code an LLM produces, and no technique's effect on NF quality is evaluated. The paper measures security of LLM-agent patches (Bandit plus manual confirmation) only to build a corpus of failures.
extraction.title: Where Did the Repair First Go Wrong? Localizing the Origins of Silent Failures in Agentic Vulnerability Repair
extraction.notes: The paper is an observational/diagnostic study of silent failures in six agent frameworks across six base models on SecurityEval and CVEfixes. SAGE is an LLM-judge localization method, not a code-improvement intervention. It reports a security assessment of agent patches (Bandit L2 screening, L3 rule-based exploitability screening, manual TP/FP confirmation), but with no intervention comparison, so it is listed as context. A reviewer could argue for 'adjacent' because the agents repair human-written vulnerable code. Venue and type fields are left empty per the exclusion rule; the paper itself is an arXiv preprint.

extraction.eligibility_reason: The paper proposes a steering technique (MRepE) intended to improve readability, but it never measures the readability of code the LLM actually generates. Outcomes are the probability of yes/no answers to readability-judgment queries, NLL ratios of fixed readable vs unreadable code snippets, and multiple-choice correctness judgments.
extraction.title: Towards the Readability of LLM-Generated Codes through Multitask Representation Engineering
extraction.notes: Borderline case. The technique is activation steering, an in-decoding intervention targeting readability (comment density, naming, cyclomatic complexity). However, all evaluation uses proxies: the model's judgment probabilities and the likelihood of pre-written MBPP-CR snippets. No generated code is scored with static tools or by humans. Correctness is likewise measured as multiple-choice accuracy on MBPP-CC. Figures are garbled in the extracted text. A reviewer should confirm that no generated-code readability metric appears in the appendix.

extraction.eligibility_reason: Proposes a framework combining security rule embedding in the prompt with an ESLint-guided LLM repair loop for LLM-generated UI code, and reports quantitative security outcomes (static finding reduction). Only the abstract was available.

extraction.eligibility_reason: Empirical study of how prompt natural language (English vs Chinese/Hindi/Spanish/Italian) affects LLM-generated code quality. extraction.eligibility_reason: Based on the abstract only, the primary outcome is robustness to prompt injection, i.e., adversarial manipulation. extraction.eligibility_reason: The paper evaluates specification form and granularity as a prompting technique for LLM code generation. If usability measures readability, re-classify as include, with family 'prompting' and stage 'pre-generation'.

extraction.eligibility_reason: Only the title is available. It describes using LLM agents as judges to assess code quality: an evaluation method, not a technique that changes the code an LLM produces. No evidence of an intervention on LLM-generated code with NF outcomes.

extraction.notes: No abstract and no full text, so the decision rests on the title alone. A reviewer should check the full text. If the multi-agent judging is used to refine LLM-generated code and NF metrics are reported, the paper could qualify. It is possibly an evaluation-methodology (context) paper instead.

extraction.eligibility_reason: The only quantitative outcome is an 'architectural violation rate' over 5 checkpoints. Every checkpoint audited is a business-rule invariant or policy guard, which is functional correctness rather than a readability, efficiency or security dimension. The enforcement call sites are also produced deterministically by the SysMARA compiler, not by the LLM.
extraction.title: AI-Readable Architecture: A New Abstraction Layer for AI-Augmented Software Development
extraction.notes: Borderline case. The paper frames violations as architectural (module boundaries, which would be maintainability). However, no module-boundary violation was measured in the experiment, only invariant and policy guard omissions. Evidence is weak: one model (Claude), 5 checkpoints, author-only audit, and the author has a conflict of interest as creator of SysMARA. A reviewer may instead argue for inclusion under readability-maintainability.

extraction.eligibility_reason: The record is a Zenodo deposit of code and research artifacts, not a full paper of 4+ pages. The topic itself fits: sparse activation interventions that reduce scanner-observed CWE vulnerabilities in LLM-generated code. Only the abstract was available, so this decision is provisional.

If an accompanying full paper exists, it would likely be eligible: an in-decoding activation-steering technique targeting security, measured with a static scanner on CWE vulnerabilities. A reviewer should search for a companion paper or preprint and re-screen it if found.

extraction.eligibility_reason: The main contribution is an assurance/admission benchmark and detector pipeline, evaluated mostly on author-built mutants. It does not change the code an LLM produces. extraction.notes: Borderline case. The paper compares an assurance-aware prompt against an interface-only prompt for generated plugins. The outcomes are parse, P0 and full-conformance yields. Defect-family prevalence (privacy, lifecycle, etc.) is reported only for a post-hoc, rule-based (non-LLM) bounded-repair stratum. The detector-recall results concern a detection pipeline, not improvement of generated code.
